name: Municipally owned electricity distribution company in Ontario (about 350,000 customers)
modelled_on: Hydro Ottawa Limited (City of Ottawa, through Hydro Ottawa Holding Inc.), using its OEB scorecard, OEB yearbook data, 2021-2025 rate application summaries, annual report and news releases; OEB yearbook peers (Elexicon Energy, London Hydro) checked for scale only
sector: electric utilities: power distribution (regulated local distribution company)
summary: This is a local electricity distribution company owned by a city through a holding company, serving about 346,000 residential, commercial and industrial customers over 1,116 square kilometres of urban, suburban and rural territory in Ontario. It takes power from the transmitter's transformer stations and delivers it through 91 substations, about 5,900 circuit kilometres of overhead and underground line, 47,000 transformers and 49,000 poles to homes and businesses. Customers pay one bill that includes the commodity, transmission and regulatory charges, but the company keeps only the distribution charge, under 20% of the bill, which the Ontario Energy Board sets through five-year rate applications and annual updates; the rest passes through to the IESO and others. Its revenue is about $184M a year of distribution revenue on $1.17B of total billings, with about $83M of operating costs and over $100M a year of capital investment. It is organised into distribution operations (line, cable and station crews and a 24-hour control room), asset management and engineering, customer service (contact centre, billing, collections and metering), finance and regulatory affairs, and corporate services, with about 570 employees, most of the trades and inside staff in one union. Its work is driven by customer growth, aging assets, storms and the Distribution System Code's service standards.

process_map.name: Respond to trouble calls and hazards
process_map.description: A trouble responder on a single-person truck is dispatched by the control room to every outage or hazard report: no power at one home, a wire down, a tree on a line, a car into a pole. The responder makes the site safe, fixes simple problems such as a blown transformer fuse or a damaged service drop, and calls for a crew when the damage is larger. Calls cluster at night and in storms, when trouble trucks are the first and often only resource on the road.

evidence.note: Cause codes from src2 and outage management and mobile workforce systems from src3; order volume is the author's estimate.

surge.cause: major storm (wind, ice, lightning or derecho)

evidence.note: Nine major events in 2019-2022 (3, 2, 1, 3 a year); most lasted under a day, the derecho took about 7 days to restore 90% of customers and caused 1,000 outages against 200 for the 2018 tornadoes. Multiplier range is the author's estimate.

process_map.name: Restore unplanned outages
process_map.description: When an outage needs more than a trouble responder, the control room isolates the damaged section and transfers customers to other feeders where it can, and a line or cable crew repairs broken poles, failed transformers and downed conductors. The OMS tracks customers out and estimated restoration times, and each event is closed with a cause code for reliability reporting. Defective equipment, loss of supply from the transmitter and foreign interference caused most customer interruptions in 2020.
process_map.unit_of_work: one outage event needing a crew

evidence.note: 2020 customer interruptions outside major events by cause (src2): defective equipment 94,236, loss of supply 64,759, foreign interference 55,962, unknown 33,536, scheduled 22,520, tree contacts 18,548. Event count is the author's estimate.

surge.cause: major storm (wind, ice, lightning or derecho)

evidence.note: Nine major events in 2019-2022; the May 2022 derecho caused 1,000 outages (against 200 for the 2018 tornadoes) and took about 7 days to restore 90% of customers with about 450 workers. Multiplier range is the author's estimate.

process_map.name: Run storm and major event response
process_map.description: When a storm overwhelms normal restoration, the utility declares a major event, opens an emergency operations centre, calls in all line, cable and support staff, contractors and crews from other utilities, and restores in priority order: hazards, hospitals and critical services, whole feeders and then single customers. The May 2022 derecho affected 180,000 customers with more than 1,000 outages and about 400 damaged poles, and restoration took about ten days with 600 workers in the field. Materials, vehicles, meals, lodging and customer communications all scale up at once. In 2019 to 2022 there were nine major events: five were losses of supply from Hydro One, three opened the incident command centre, and only the May 2022 derecho used mutual aid.

evidence.note: Volume from edu-ops-major-event-response (2026-11-24): Nine major events in 48 months (three in 2019, two in 2020, one in 2021, three in 2022) = 0.19 a month; low and high reflect one and four events a year.

process_map.name: Monitor and operate the distribution grid
process_map.description: System operators watch SCADA alarms, feeder loading and the OMS around the clock, group incoming outage calls into predicted outages, dispatch trouble responders and crews, and operate remote switches to restore customers. They coordinate with the transmitter's control centre when a transformer station or supply circuit trips. Night and weekend shifts carry the same desk with fewer people, and storms flood the desk with hundreds of events.

evidence.note: System control and outage management systems (src3); loss of supply was a top outage cause in 2021 (src1). Shift count assumes two 12-hour shifts a day.

surge.cause: major storm or transmission supply loss

evidence.note: Nine major events in 2019-2022, most under a day; operators were held past shift and a storm desk added. The multiplier is the author's estimate of extra operator-shifts: the number of shifts does not change, but extended and overlapping shifts add 10% to 100% more desk hours.

process_map.name: Plan and execute switching for planned work
process_map.description: Every planned job on energized or isolatable plant needs a switching order: a switching planner writes the sequence from the GIS network model, a second person checks it, and on the day the system operator directs field staff step by step and issues a work protection permit before anyone works. Orders are booked days ahead around load limits and customer outages. Errors can injure workers or drop customers, so steps are checked twice and recorded.

evidence.note: Common practice of Ontario distributors under utility work protection codes; order volume estimated from crew numbers and the capital program.

surge.cause: rebuild after a major storm (for example the May 2022 derecho) adds planned switching for permanent repairs

evidence.note: Author's estimate; temporary storm repairs are later rebuilt as planned work under switching orders.

process_map.name: Plan and schedule field work
process_map.description: Work planners take released capital, maintenance and customer work orders, check that design, materials, permits, locates and switching are ready, and build weekly and daily crew schedules. They rebalance the plan every day as trouble, storms, absences and customer delays pull crews away. Jobs that are not ready when the crew arrives are the main source of lost crew time.

evidence.note: Typical planning practice; order volume estimated from about 60 crews and staff doing several orders a week.

surge.cause: major storm pulls crews to restoration and forces the planned schedule to be rebuilt

evidence.note: Author's estimate; the organisation file assumes one to four declared major events a year. During a storm planned work stops and every scheduled order is rescheduled, so planner workload multiplies.

process_map.name: Build overhead capital work
process_map.description: Line crews build the overhead part of capital projects: new pole lines for growth, rebuilds of aging rear-lot and rural lines, and transformer and switch replacements. A typical job takes a four-person crew with a bucket truck and a digger derrick from one to several days, under a work protection permit and after locates. Weather, road occupancy permits, customer access and missing materials hold jobs up.

evidence.note: 23% of overhead assets past expected life (src5); renewal and growth investments (src4). Job counts are the author's estimate.

surge.cause: autumn push to finish the year's capital program before freeze-up

evidence.note: Common practice for capital programs funded on a calendar year; multiplier is the author's estimate.

process_map.name: Build and renew underground plant
process_map.description: Cable crews install and replace underground primary cable, padmount transformers, switchgear and vaults, splice and terminate cable after contractors have built the ducts, and energize new subdivisions. Cable replacement is a large share of renewal spending. Jobs depend on civil contractors finishing on time, on locates, on switching and on booked customer outages.

evidence.note: Three-year cost per metre of underground cable is a custom scorecard measure (src5); volumes are the author's estimate.

surge.cause: autumn push to energize new subdivisions and finish cable renewal before frost

evidence.note: Builders and capital programs aim to finish before winter; multiplier is the author's estimate.

process_map.name: Replace poles
process_map.description: Poles found in poor condition by inspection and testing are replaced in a planned program of about 325 to 350 poles a year: the crew sets a new pole beside the old one, transfers conductors and equipment, and removes the old pole once telecom attachers have moved their cables. Attacher transfers often leave stub poles standing for months. Storms add hundreds of broken poles in a few days.

evidence.note: 325-350 poles a year in a normal year (src6).

surge.cause: follow-up after a major storm (temporary repairs made permanent, stubs and leaning poles)

evidence.note: About 400 poles to repair or replace after the May 2022 storm (source); those were replaced as emergency restoration, so the surge here covers only the planned follow-up work, the author's estimate. The organisation file's multiplier of up to 40 counts the storm replacements themselves.

process_map.name: Connect and energize new services
process_map.description: Once the customer has paid, the electrician's wiring has passed ESA inspection and the meter is ready, a crew connects and energizes the service: an overhead drop from a pole or an underground service from a padmount transformer. The Distribution System Code requires a low-voltage connection within five business days of all conditions being met at least 90% of the time; 5,024 were connected in 2021, all on time. Missing ESA authorizations and unfinished customer work are the usual reasons a booking moves.

evidence.note: Volume from edu-ops-service-connection-work (2026-11-24): 5,024 low-voltage connections in 2021 (scorecard), about 420 a month; Hydro Ottawa reports residential customer connections averaging 6,067 a year in 2021-2023 (DSP overview), about 505 a month, so the high case is raised to 560 from the organisation file's 520.

surge.cause: backlog of rebooked connections after a major storm pulls all crews to restoration

evidence.note: Author's estimate; the organisation file uses the May 2022 derecho (about ten days) as the large ordinary storm, and the scorecard says missed appointments come mainly from emergencies and weather.

process_map.name: Inspect and maintain substations
process_map.description: Station electricians inspect the 91 substations monthly and maintain power transformers, breakers, switchgear, batteries and buildings on time-based and condition-based cycles, with oil sampling and infrared scans. Major work needs a station or transformer out of service, often backed by a mobile substation, and is booked around seasonal peaks. About half of the stations had passed their expected service life when the 2021-2025 plan was written.

evidence.note: Volume from edu-ops-station-maintenance (2026-11-24): About 91-92 stations (source says 92 in 2021) inspected monthly gives about 91 routine work orders a month; 25 to 40 outage maintenance orders a month (transformers, breakers, switchgear, batteries) is the author's estimate for a fleet of about 90 stations with roughly 180 power transformers. Agrees with the organisation file's range.

process_map.name: Test and commission protection and control
process_map.description: Protection and control technologists test and commission relays, reclosers, station RTUs and feeder automation devices, apply the settings issued by engineering, and investigate misoperations after faults. New stations and automation projects add commissioning peaks. Settings errors can cause wide outages or leave faults uncleared, so test records are kept for every device.
process_map.unit_of_work: one protection test or commissioning job

evidence.note: Typical practice; volume is the author's estimate.

process_map.name: Locate and repair underground cable faults
process_map.description: When an underground cable fails, the control room isolates the section and a cable crew finds the fault with time-domain reflectometry and a thumper, excavates or calls a hydrovac contractor, and splices or replaces the cable. Many faults are on aging direct-buried cable in older subdivisions, where customers can be out for hours while the fault is found. Repeated faults on the same cable feed the renewal program.

evidence.note: Volume from edu-ops-cable-fault-repair (2026-11-24): About 5,000 km (3,100 miles) of cable (tdw2016) at EPRI's median of 1.9 failures per 100 conductor miles per year for cable, joints and terminations gives about 60 a year; aged 1970s-1990 XLPE plausibly fails three to four times the median, giving about 15 to 25 a month with dig-ins. Seasonality from mb_cable. The organisation file's 25-40-70 a month looks high for primary cable faults.

surge.cause: summer heat wave or thaw period with clustered cable failures

evidence.note: Faults are more frequent when the ground thaws in spring and summer (source); event counts and multiplier are the author's estimate.

process_map.name: Inspect overhead and underground plant
process_map.description: Overhead lines, poles, padmount transformers and underground equipment are inspected on a fixed multi-year cycle by patrol, pole testing and infrared scans. Inspectors record deficiencies on tablets with photos and a priority, and urgent hazards such as a leaning pole or an open padmount go straight to a crew. The findings drive maintenance work orders, ESA due diligence records and the asset condition data.
process_map.unit_of_work: one asset inspected (a pole with its overhead equipment, or one ground-level unit such as a pad-mounted transformer, switchgear or vault)

evidence.note: Volume from edu-ops-distribution-inspection (2026-11-24): About 38,946 transformers inspected regularly and 49,000 poles tested at 10-year intervals (ho_grids2024); routine inspection on a three-year cycle across the territory (ho_grid2024). Estimate per year: 16,300 pole visual inspections (49,000 / 3), 4,900 pole tests, about 8,300 ground-level transformers (about 25,000 pad-mounted / 3) and about 1,000 switchgear and vaults: about 30,500 a year or 2,500 a month. The organisation file's mode of 1,800 implies a longer cycle than the sources state.

process_map.name: Manage tree trimming near lines
process_map.description: Tree contractors trim around overhead lines on a multi-year cycle by circuit, with a coordinator planning circuits, notifying property owners, handling refusals and checking completed work before the invoice is paid. Tree contacts caused 18,548 customer interruptions in 2020 outside major events, and falling trees caused most damage in the 2022 storm. Urgent trims after patrols or customer calls are dispatched outside the cycle.
process_map.unit_of_work: one circuit-kilometre trimmed on cycle, or one urgent tree request between cycles

evidence.note: Volume from edu-ops-vegetation-management (2026-11-24): Two-year urban and three-year rural cycles (tdw2026) over about 2,746 km of overhead line (organisation file) give about 1,000 to 1,100 km a year, or 85 to 95 km a month; more than 60,000 trees a year (ho_grids2024) is about 55 to 60 trees per km. About 40 urgent requests a month from inspections and customer calls is the author's estimate. The organisation file's 75 a month counts cycle km only and sits a little low for these cycles.

surge.cause: major storm (wind, ice storm, tornado or derecho)

evidence.note: The May 2022 derecho put more than 180,000 customers out and compressed about four years of emergency repairs into 14 days (source); frequency and multiplier for urgent tree work are the author's estimates.

process_map.name: Locate underground plant for excavators
process_map.description: Ontario One Call sends every dig notification in the service area to the utility; requests clear of plant are screened out and cable locators mark the rest with paint and flags or issue a clearance, within five business days for standard requests. Spring and summer volumes exceed in-house capacity, so overflow goes to a locate contractor. Late locates hold up excavators and the utility's own crews, and wrong marks lead to cable strikes and public contacts.

evidence.note: Five-business-day deadline under the Ontario Underground Infrastructure Notification System Act, 2012 is from general knowledge (the statute page could not be opened); volume is the author's estimate for a city of one million. Revised 2026-11-24: most locates are marked by contract locators (contract-locator, contractor staff); in-house locators handle complex and urgent jobs.

surge.cause: spring start of construction, when frozen-season backlog and new projects arrive together

evidence.note: Author's estimate; the organisation file describes spring and summer volumes exceeding in-house capacity.

process_map.name: Carry out field service orders
process_map.description: Field service representatives carry out disconnections and reconnections for non-payment and move-outs where remote switching is not available, investigate high-bill and voltage complaints, check suspected tampering and do service checks. Appointments that need the customer present must be offered in a four-hour window and kept at least 90% of the time; 9,001 were booked in 2021. Disconnections for arrears stop for residential customers from mid-November to the end of April.

evidence.note: Appointment standard and 9,001 appointments (src1); winter ban (src10). Order volume is the author's estimate.

surge.cause: end of the winter disconnection ban releases a backlog of residential arrears disconnections

evidence.note: The ban ends each April 30; the size of the backlog is the author's estimate.

process_map.name: Notify customers of planned outages
process_map.description: For each planned outage the dispatch team identifies affected customers from the GIS connectivity model, delivers notices or sends calls and emails several days ahead, and books critical customers such as medical equipment users and businesses around the work. Rescheduling for weather means repeating the notices. Scheduled outages caused 22,520 customer interruptions in 2020.

evidence.note: Scheduled outage interruptions from src2; outage count is the author's estimate.

process_map.name: Isolate lines for customers and contractors
process_map.description: Builders, roofers, tree companies and sign installers ask the utility to disconnect a service or cover lines so they can work safely near them. Dispatch books the job, the control room issues protection where needed, and a crew installs line covers or opens the service and restores it on the agreed date. Charges follow the specific service charges in the tariff.

evidence.note: Typical service; volume is the author's estimate.

process_map.name: Lay out residential and small business services
process_map.description: A residential or small business customer, or their electrician, applies for a new, upgraded or relocated service. A design technologist checks transformer and secondary capacity, visits the site if needed, issues a service layout with any customer charges, and once the customer pays and the site is ready creates the work order for the crew. Waiting for the customer's electrician and the ESA inspection takes most of the elapsed time.

evidence.note: Service layouts are among the 9,001 appointments in 2021 (src1); request volume assumes some requests do not proceed.

process_map.name: Connect subdivisions and large developments
process_map.description: Developers of subdivisions, condominiums and commercial buildings apply for supply. Engineering checks feeder and station capacity, designs the distribution layout, runs the economic evaluation required by the Distribution System Code to set the customer's capital contribution, and negotiates the connection or subdivision agreement. After payment the developer's contractor builds civil works under inspection, and utility crews install and energize cable and transformers.

evidence.note: System Access spending of $56.7M planned for 2021 against $39.2M of capital contributions (src5); project count is the author's estimate.

process_map.name: Connect generation and storage
process_map.description: Customers and developers apply to connect rooftop solar, battery storage and larger generators. Micro-embedded projects of 10 kW or less must be connected within five business days once conditions are met; larger projects get a connection impact assessment within 60 to 90 days and then an offer to connect. In 2021 the utility connected 52 micro-embedded generators and completed six assessments totalling 11.6 MW, all on time.

evidence.note: Volumes and time standards from src1.

process_map.name: Forecast load and plan capacity
process_map.description: Planning engineers forecast feeder and station loads from growth, development applications and electrification, compare them with planning capacity, and propose new feeders, station expansions and load transfers. They take part in regional planning with the transmitter and the IESO for transformer station capacity. Their studies feed the Distribution System Plan and set where new customers can connect.
process_map.unit_of_work: one planning study (area, station, feeder or regional planning input)

evidence.note: Stations and feeders exceeding planning capacity are custom scorecard measures (src5); study count is the author's estimate.

process_map.name: Assess asset condition and risk
process_map.description: Asset analysts combine inspection results, test data, age, failure history and loading into a health index for each asset class, estimate failure risk and rank renewal candidates. In 2019 about 19% of assets had reached expected service life, including 51% of stations and 23% of overhead assets, and 17% were in poor or very poor condition. The ranking drives the renewal budget and the pole, cable and station programs.
process_map.unit_of_work: one annual asset condition assessment across 12 major asset classes

evidence.note: Asset demographic and condition figures from src5.

process_map.name: Build the capital plan and Distribution System Plan
process_map.description: Each year engineering turns planning studies, asset condition, connection forecasts, city road works and general plant needs into a capital program by OEB investment category, paced to the rate plan and to crew and contractor capacity. Every five years the program becomes the Distribution System Plan filed with the rate application; the 2021-2025 plan averaged about $100.8M net a year. Executive and board approval fix the budget, and progress is reported as DSP implementation on the scorecard (92% in 2021).
process_map.unit_of_work: one annual capital program (and, one year in five, the Distribution System Plan)

evidence.note: Capital by category from src5; DSP implementation 92% in 2021 (src1).

process_map.name: Deliver capital projects
process_map.description: Project managers turn released capital projects into designs, permits, contracts, materials, outage bookings and crew time, track cost and schedule, and close projects so they can be capitalized. Projects compete with customer connections and trouble work for the same crews, and in 2021 labour and material shortages and pandemic outage limits deferred part of the plan. Civil work is mostly contracted and inspected; electrical work is done by in-house crews.

evidence.note: DSP implementation progress and reasons for the 2021 deferrals from src1; project counts are the author's estimate.

surge.cause: major storm leaving rebuild and replacement projects (for example the May 2022 derecho)

evidence.note: The derecho damaged more than 500 poles and added $15.3M of capital, four years of emergency replacements in two weeks; the follow-on permanent rebuild share and duration are the author's estimate.

process_map.name: Design capital and renewal projects
process_map.description: Design technologists produce construction drawings, bills of materials and estimates for capital and renewal projects from field surveys and the GIS model, apply construction standards, and obtain municipal consents and road permits. Designs are reviewed by a supervisor and, for complex work, sealed by an engineer. Changes found in the field come back for redesign.

evidence.note: Typical; volume is the author's estimate.

process_map.name: Inspect contractor construction
process_map.description: Construction inspectors visit contractor sites building ducts, vaults, transformer pads and pole lines, check work against standards and drawings, and accept or reject it before utility crews install cable and equipment. Deficiencies go back to the contractor. Accepted quantities support contractor progress payments.

evidence.note: Typical; volume is the author's estimate.

process_map.name: Post as-builts and maintain the GIS
process_map.description: GIS technicians post as-built drawings from completed jobs into the GIS and ERP asset register, update the network connectivity used by the OMS and control room, and fix data errors reported from the field. Backlogs of unposted as-builts mean the control room and designers work from out-of-date maps. Every new service, transformer, pole and cable section passes through this queue.

evidence.note: GIS named in src3; volume is the author's estimate.

process_map.name: Maintain construction standards and approved materials
process_map.description: Standards engineers maintain construction standards and approved material specifications, evaluate new products, respond to field feedback and ESA findings, and approve design changes. Approved designs and equipment are a requirement of O. Reg. 22/04. Supply problems often force quick approval of substitute materials.

evidence.note: O. Reg. 22/04 compliance confirmed by ESA audits (src1); revision count is the author's estimate.

process_map.name: Process pole attachment requests
process_map.description: Telecom companies apply to attach fibre and cable to poles. A technologist checks pole loading and clearances, specifies make-ready work such as taller poles or rearranged equipment, bills the attacher and issues a permit, and transfers after pole replacements are tracked until the old pole can be removed. Fibre and wireless rollouts produce bursts of applications.

evidence.note: Typical; volume is the author's estimate.

process_map.name: Relocate plant for road and transit works
process_map.description: When the city widens roads, renews sewers or builds light rail, the utility must move poles, cable and equipment, with costs shared under provincial rules for utilities on public roads. Project managers agree scope, cost sharing and timing, then run the relocation like a capital project. City schedules change often, which leaves crews and materials waiting.

evidence.note: Support for light rail is a planned initiative (src4); volume is the author's estimate.

process_map.name: Analyze reliability
process_map.description: An engineer validates outage records from the OMS, checks cause codes, separates loss of supply and major events, and calculates SAIDI, SAIFI and worst-performing feeders each month and for the annual filing. In 2021 customers averaged 0.83 hours and 0.62 interruptions, excluding loss of supply and major events. Findings go to capital planning and targeted maintenance.

evidence.note: Reliability results from src1 and src2.

process_map.name: Set protection and coordination
process_map.description: Protection engineers run coordination studies and issue relay and recloser settings for new stations, feeder changes and generator connections, and review misoperations reported by technologists. Generator connections increasingly change fault levels and need new settings. Settings are kept in a protection database with version control.

evidence.note: Typical; volume is the author's estimate.

process_map.name: Answer customer calls and contacts
process_map.description: Customer service representatives answer calls, emails, web forms and chat about bills, payments, moves, outages, new services and complaints, using the CIS, the OMS and the web portal. The OEB standard is 65% of calls answered within 30 seconds; in 2021 agents took 186,632 calls, answered 83.14% on time and resolved 89% at first contact. Storms and rate changes bring call spikes that the IVR and outage map only partly absorb.
process_map.unit_of_work: one customer call answered by an agent

evidence.note: Call volume, service level and first-contact resolution from src1; Saturday hours from src5.

surge.cause: major storm (wind, ice storm, tornado or derecho)

evidence.note: The May 2022 derecho caused more than 1,000 outages, five times the 2018 tornadoes, with restoration over about ten days (src6, src7); 2021 had one major event (src1). Frequency and multiplier ranges are the author's estimate.

process_map.name: Open and close customer accounts
process_map.description: When a customer moves in or out, the account is closed or opened in the CIS with a reading on the move date from the smart meter, a security deposit is assessed for new non-residential customers or those without good credit history, and landlords' default accounts pick up vacant units. New services energized by crews also create accounts. Late or missing move notices produce bills to the wrong person and later corrections.
process_map.unit_of_work: one move request (move-out, move-in or both at one premise) or new-service account

evidence.note: Author's estimate: 15-20% of residential accounts change occupant each year, peaking in summer and at month ends.

process_map.name: Collect and validate smart meter data
process_map.description: Each day the AMI head-end collects hourly reads from about 350,000 smart meters and sends them to the provincial Meter Data Management/Repository, which validates, estimates and edits the data and returns billing quantities. Meter data analysts work the exceptions: meters not communicating, failed validations and register mismatches, and send field orders when a meter must be visited. Unresolved exceptions become estimated bills.

evidence.note: Several hundred thousand smart meters and the provincial Smart Metering Entity (src3); exception rates are the author's estimate.

process_map.name: Bill customers monthly
process_map.description: The CIS bills about 350,000 customers monthly in daily cycles, applying OEB-approved distribution rates, the commodity price under the Regulated Price Plan or a retailer contract, transmission and regulatory charges, rebates and HST to the validated reads. Bills that pass validation are printed or posted online; more than 60% of customers were paperless by 2021. The OEB standard is 98% billing accuracy, and the utility reported 99.88% on more than 4.2 million bills in 2021.

evidence.note: Bill count and accuracy from src1; paperless share from src11.

process_map.name: Resolve billing exceptions
process_map.description: Bills that fail validation are held: very high or low consumption, estimated reads, missing meter changes, rate class or retailer mismatches. Billing analysts investigate in the CIS and meter data, correct and release the bill, cancel and rebill earlier periods when needed, and send field orders when a meter must be checked. Holds that age past the billing window break the monthly billing requirement and generate calls.
process_map.unit_of_work: one held bill or billing investigation

evidence.note: Billing accuracy standard and result from src1; an exception rate of about 1.5-2.5% of bills is the author's estimate.

process_map.name: Apply customer payments
process_map.description: Payments arrive daily from banks, pre-authorized debits, card processors, cheques and payment agents. The CIS loads remittance files automatically, and a billing analyst reconciles totals to the bank deposit and applies unidentified, misdirected and returned payments by hand. Errors here trigger wrong collection notices.
process_map.unit_of_work: one daily payment file and its exceptions

evidence.note: Typical; daily cycle.

process_map.name: Collect overdue accounts
process_map.description: The CIS ages unpaid balances and issues reminders and disconnection notices under the OEB's customer service rules, which require notice periods, offers of arrears payment agreements and extra protection for eligible low-income customers. Collections representatives call customers, set up payment agreements, assess security deposits, and order disconnections or load limiters, which are barred for residential customers from November 15 to April 30. Disconnections were suspended for long periods during the pandemic, so arrears grew in 2020 and 2021.
process_map.unit_of_work: one account in arrears (one overdue bill episode)

evidence.note: Winter ban (src10); hardship payment plans during COVID-19 (src3). Volume is the author's estimate.

surge.cause: end of the winter disconnection ban (and in 2020 the end of the extended pandemic ban), when held residential arrears move to disconnection notices

evidence.note: Ban dates from the sources; size of the spring wave is the author's estimate.

process_map.name: Resolve complaints and escalations
process_map.description: Complaints that front-line agents cannot resolve go to a supervisor or customer relations specialist, who investigates billing, outage, damage or service issues, replies in writing and tracks the case to closure. Complaints referred by the OEB have fixed response times and are reported. Recurring themes go to the business areas concerned.

evidence.note: Typical; volume is the author's estimate.

process_map.name: Process retailer transactions
process_map.description: When a customer signs with a licensed retailer, the retailer sends an enrolment through the EBT hub; the billing team validates it, switches the account at the next read and bills the retailer's price, and drops, changes and rejections follow the same route. Retailer amounts are settled monthly. Only a small share of customers buy from retailers.

evidence.note: Typical; volume is the author's estimate.

process_map.name: Apply low-income assistance
process_map.description: Customers in hardship are referred to the Ontario Electricity Support Program, whose approved credits are applied to their monthly bills, and to LEAP emergency financial assistance, which social agencies administer partly with distributor funds. Collections staff apply credits, hold collection action while applications are pending and offer longer payment agreements. Pandemic relief programs added temporary credits in 2020 and 2021.

evidence.note: Hardship payment plans (src3) and more than $1M of relief funding in 2021 (src11); OESP and LEAP rules from general knowledge; volume is the author's estimate.

process_map.name: Install and exchange meters
process_map.description: Meter technicians install meters for new services, exchange failed and non-communicating meters, replace meters whose Measurement Canada seal period has expired, and install bidirectional meters for generators. Each exchange records old and new meter numbers and readings, which must reach the CIS and the provincial repository before the next bill. Large commercial meters with instrument transformers need two technicians and an outage or bypass.

evidence.note: Seal and reverification rules from general knowledge; volume is the author's estimate.

surge.cause: Measurement Canada sampling failure or seal expiry of a large meter lot, forcing a replacement campaign

evidence.note: Lots that reach the end of their reverification period without a sampling extension must be removed from service (e26); size and frequency are the author's estimate.

process_map.name: Test and sample meters
process_map.description: The meter shop receives new meters, tests samples from each shipment, and runs Measurement Canada sampling of in-service meter groups so a group's seal can be extended instead of replacing every meter. Groups that fail sampling must be replaced, which creates a large exchange program. Failed meters returned from the field are tested before disposal or warranty claims.
process_map.unit_of_work: one meter lot or sample test

evidence.note: Measurement Canada sampling rules from general knowledge; volume is the author's estimate.

process_map.name: Serve key account customers
process_map.description: Key account representatives look after large users, federal and institutional campuses and large commercial customers: they coordinate planned outages, explain bills and global adjustment, follow up outages and power quality complaints, and bring large load additions to engineering early. The formal Key Accounts program is one of the utility's regular engagement channels.

evidence.note: Key Accounts program (src5); 3,256 customers above 50 kW and 11 large users (src2). Volume is the author's estimate.

process_map.name: Settle with the IESO
process_map.description: Each month the settlement analyst pays the IESO invoice for wholesale energy, global adjustment and market charges, and submits the Regulated Price Plan settlement and global adjustment allocations that reconcile what customers were billed with what the market charged. Errors flow into retail settlement variance accounts that the OEB later reviews. Cost of power, about $984M in 2020, passes through to customers but must be reconciled exactly.

evidence.note: Cost of power and related costs $983.9M in 2020 (src2); settlement steps from general knowledge.

process_map.name: Prepare the rebasing rate application
process_map.description: Every five years the utility files a Custom Incentive Rate-setting application covering its business plan, Distribution System Plan, OM&A, rate base, cost of capital, load forecast, cost allocation and rate design. Intervenors and OEB staff send written interrogatories, the parties hold a settlement conference, and the OEB issues a decision and rate order; the 2021-2025 application asked for a 2021 service revenue requirement of $216.6M. Nearly every department works on it for more than a year.

evidence.note: Application contents and amounts from src5; customer engagement of nearly 21,000 customers from src4. Revised 2026-11-24: the OEB backgrounder gives a proposed 2021 base revenue requirement of $203.9 million; the description's $216.6 million may be the service revenue requirement, as the edu-09 workflow author noted.

process_map.name: File the annual rate update and load tariffs
process_map.description: Between rebasing applications the utility files an annual update that applies the approved escalation, updates retail transmission service rates and disposes of variance account balances, then loads the new tariff into the CIS for the effective date. Rate changes must be tested in the CIS before they go live, and customers are told about bill impacts.

evidence.note: Annual OM&A escalation under the Custom IR plan (src5); steps typical.

process_map.name: File OEB reporting and scorecard
process_map.description: Under the OEB's Reporting and Record-keeping Requirements the utility files service quality and reliability data during the year and financial statements, customer and asset statistics annually, which the OEB publishes in its yearbook and scorecard. Regulatory analysts gather the data from the CIS, OMS, ERP and HR systems, reconcile it, file through the OEB portal and write the scorecard commentary. Late or inconsistent filings draw OEB compliance follow-up.
process_map.unit_of_work: one RRR return (one section due on one deadline, or the scorecard MD&A)

evidence.note: Volume from edu-fin-rrr-reporting (2026-11-24): Count of distributor reporting sections and deadlines in s1 (about 21 a year); MD&A timing from s2. High case allows for ad hoc reports (2.1.18, 2.1.21) and data revisions.

process_map.name: Close the books
process_map.description: Accountants post billing, settlement, payables, payroll, inventory and work order entries, accrue unbilled revenue and unbilled power costs, reconcile the bank and regulatory accounts, and produce monthly results for management and the parent company. Year-end adds the external audit. Late cost postings from field work orders are a frequent cause of adjustments.

evidence.note: Financial statements reported in RRR (src2); steps typical.

process_map.name: Pay suppliers and contractors
process_map.description: Supplier and contractor invoices are matched to purchase orders and receipts or to certified progress quantities, coded to work orders, approved and paid by EFT. Contractor invoices for civil work, tree trimming and storm support need field certification before payment, which is the usual cause of delay.

evidence.note: Typical; volume is the author's estimate.

process_map.name: Run payroll
process_map.description: Payroll clerks process biweekly pay for about 570 staff from crew time entries, which include overtime, standby, call-out and shift premiums under the IBEW collective agreement. Storms create heavy overtime that must be keyed and checked within the pay period. Labour charges are posted to work orders for capitalization.

evidence.note: IBEW agreement (src8); pay cycle assumed.

process_map.name: Prepare the budget and forecasts
process_map.description: Each autumn finance builds the next year's OM&A and capital budget with each division, within the rate plan and the board's dividend and debt targets, and refreshes forecasts quarterly. The capital plan from engineering is the largest input. Gaps between rates and costs are closed by deferring programs or finding productivity savings.

evidence.note: OM&A by category and the escalation approach (src5).

process_map.name: Buy materials and services
process_map.description: Buyers source poles, cable, transformers, meters and hardware under multi-year agreements and tenders, and contract civil, tree, locate and construction services. Requisitions come from stores replenishment and project managers; long lead times for transformers and switchgear, which grew in 2021 and 2022, force early ordering. Public-sector style tendering rules apply to a municipally owned company.

evidence.note: Material availability deferred planned work in 2021 (src1); order volume is the author's estimate.

surge.cause: major storm restoration (emergency buys of poles, transformers, conductor and contractor crews)

evidence.note: Emergency spending above budget for poles and underground transformers in 2021 (s3); storm frequency follows the organisation file; the multiplier is the author's estimate.

process_map.name: Run stores and issue materials
process_map.description: Stores attendants receive deliveries, stage materials for scheduled jobs, issue materials to crews early in the morning and after hours for trouble, and trigger replenishment at minimum stock. During storms stores run around the clock and poles, transformers and conductor can run short. Issues are charged to work orders in the ERP.

evidence.note: Typical; issue volume is the author's estimate.

surge.cause: major storm (wind, ice storm, tornado or derecho)

evidence.note: The May 2022 derecho caused more than 1,000 outages, five times the 2018 tornadoes, with restoration over about ten days (src6, src7); 2021 had one major event (src1). Frequency and multiplier ranges are the author's estimate.

process_map.name: Track variance and deferral accounts
process_map.description: Regulatory analysts track the variance and deferral accounts the OEB allows, including retail settlement variances for power and global adjustment and pandemic-related costs in 2020 to 2022, with monthly carrying charges. Balances are tested for disposition in the annual rate update. Errors in these accounts can reverse millions of dollars of revenue later.

evidence.note: Typical practice under OEB accounting procedures; recalled from general knowledge.

process_map.name: Capitalize completed work
process_map.description: Accountants review completed capital work orders, check that labour, materials, contractor costs and capital contributions are coded correctly, and capitalize assets into the fixed asset register when they go into service. As-built records and work order completion often arrive months after energization, which delays capitalization and rate base.

evidence.note: Gross capital additions $122.9M in 2020 (src2); count is the author's estimate.

process_map.name: Manage cash, financing and insurance
process_map.description: Finance forecasts cash needs for capital and the monthly IESO payment, draws on credit facilities and long-term debt arranged through the parent company, pays dividends to the shareholder and renews insurance. The large IESO payment each month makes cash timing tight.
process_map.unit_of_work: one monthly cash and financing cycle

evidence.note: Debt to equity 1.92 and current ratio 1.00 in 2021 (src1); steps typical.

process_map.name: Recruit staff
process_map.description: HR posts approved vacancies, screens applicants, runs aptitude tests for apprentices and interviews, checks references and driver's licences, and onboards new staff. Retirements in trades and control room roles drive a steady flow of apprentice and journeyperson hiring; the pandemic froze hiring in 2020.

evidence.note: Workforce renewal and the 2020 hiring freeze (src3); volume is the author's estimate.

process_map.name: Train apprentices and keep qualifications current
process_map.description: Trades apprentices follow a multi-year program of college blocks, on-the-job hours and in-house training, and all field staff keep current qualifications in work protection, first aid, rescue and equipment operation. The coordinator tracks hours and expiry dates, and an expired qualification takes a worker off a crew. In 2020 the program had 44 apprentices, 26% of the trades workforce.
process_map.unit_of_work: one training course or qualification record

evidence.note: Apprentice numbers from src3; course volume is the author's estimate.

process_map.name: Administer the collective agreement
process_map.description: HR administers the collective agreement with the IBEW, which represents about 390 trades and inside staff: grievances, overtime and call-out disputes, seniority-based postings and bargaining. Storm overtime and call-out lists generate many disputes. The agreement in force through the period expired in March 2023.

evidence.note: Union size and expiry from src8; grievance count is the author's estimate.

process_map.name: Investigate incidents and audit safety
process_map.description: Every injury, near miss, vehicle incident and electrical contact is reported, investigated by the supervisor with a safety advisor, and closed with corrective actions; advisors also audit crews in the field and support the joint health and safety committee. High-voltage work, traffic and heavy equipment make field work hazardous, and serious incidents are reported to the Ministry of Labour. The custom scorecard tracks the all injury frequency rate and lost workday severity.
process_map.unit_of_work: one incident or one field safety audit

evidence.note: Safety measures on the custom scorecard (src5); incident counts are the author's estimate.

surge.cause: major storm restoration with long crew shifts

evidence.note: Organisation file assumption of one to four declared major events a year (May 2022 derecho as the large case). More vehicle, fatigue and near-miss incidents during restoration while planned audits stop; the multiplier is the author's estimate.

process_map.name: Comply with the distribution safety regulation
process_map.description: Under Ontario Regulation 22/04 the utility must use approved designs and equipment, inspect construction, keep records and report serious electrical incidents to the Electrical Safety Authority. Each year the utility hires an ESA-approved auditor, ESA reviews the auditor's report, and a professional engineer, director or officer signs the Declaration of Compliance. Staff prepare due diligence inspection records, answer ESA audits and public safety concerns, and report every contact with utility plant; in 2021 the utility reported 20 public contacts, none serious, and was found compliant.
process_map.unit_of_work: one ESA reportable item (incident report, ESA finding or concern, or the annual audit and declaration)

evidence.note: Regulation requirements, 20 public contacts and audit result from src1.

surge.cause: major storm with many downed lines

evidence.note: Organisation file assumption of one to four major events a year. Downed lines near the public raise reports, though contacts caused by weather that is force majeure need not be reported (esa_seir); the multiplier is the author's estimate.

process_map.name: Respond to spills and manage environmental compliance
process_map.description: Leaking or storm-damaged transformers spill mineral oil onto roads, lawns and storm drains, and some older equipment may contain PCBs. Advisors respond with spill contractors, report to the provincial spills line when required, arrange clean-up and testing, and manage disposal of oil and old equipment.

evidence.note: Typical; volume is the author's estimate.

process_map.name: Maintain the vehicle fleet
process_map.description: Fleet mechanics run preventive maintenance and annual safety inspections on about 220 vehicles, repair breakdowns, and keep aerial devices dielectric-tested and certified. A bucket truck out of service can idle a whole crew, so repairs are prioritized by crew impact. Vehicles are replaced on age and condition through the capital plan.

evidence.note: Volume from edu-corp-fleet-maintenance (2026-11-24): About 214 vehicles (organisation file resource counts) at two to four preventive services a year, one annual safety inspection for about 85 trucks over 4,500 kg (mto2021), about 70 annual dielectric tests of insulated booms (applus) and about 100 defect and breakdown repairs a month. Agrees with the organisation file's range.

surge.cause: major storm (wind, ice storm, tornado or derecho)

evidence.note: The May 2022 derecho caused more than 1,000 outages, five times the 2018 tornadoes, with restoration over about ten days (src6, src7); 2021 had one major event (src1). Frequency and multiplier ranges are the author's estimate.

process_map.name: Maintain buildings and yards
process_map.description: Facilities coordinators maintain the operations centres, office buildings, stores yards and control centre, manage cleaning, security and building systems, and handle moves and space changes through contractors. The control centre and stores need backup power and access around the clock.

evidence.note: Consolidation of staff into two new buildings (src4); request volume is the author's estimate.

process_map.name: Run the IT service desk
process_map.description: The service desk logs incidents and requests from staff, sets up accounts for new hires, supports laptops, field tablets and phones, and routes problems in the CIS, ERP and GIS to business systems analysts. Field tablet problems at the start of a shift hold up crews, so they get priority.

evidence.note: Typical; ticket volume is the author's estimate at about two tickets per employee per month.

process_map.name: Change and release business systems
process_map.description: Business systems analysts configure and release changes to the CIS, ERP, GIS and web portal: new rates each year, regulatory billing changes such as pandemic price changes, new programs and fixes. Every billing change needs testing against sample bills before release, and errors reach thousands of customers at once.

evidence.note: Systems named in src3; change volume is the author's estimate.

process_map.name: Monitor and respond to cyber threats
process_map.description: Cyber analysts monitor security alerts across corporate and operational networks, review access to SCADA and the CIS, track patching, and report against the OEB's cyber security framework. Phishing and ransomware attempts are constant, and an incident in the control network could stop remote switching.

evidence.note: Cyber risk named in src3 and src4; alert count is the author's estimate.

process_map.name: Support SCADA, OMS and metering systems
process_map.description: OT specialists keep SCADA, the OMS, the AMI head-end and the field communications network running, add new stations and devices to SCADA, and are on call when the control room loses visibility. OMS model updates from GIS have to be loaded and tested without disrupting live operations.

evidence.note: Systems named in src3; ticket volume is the author's estimate.

process_map.name: Communicate with the public and media
process_map.description: Communications advisors run public safety campaigns about overhead and underground lines, digging and tree planting, answer media questions, publish news releases, and support rate application engagement. Public awareness of electrical safety is measured by a survey (72% in 2021).

evidence.note: Safety campaigns and the 72% awareness result from src1; volume is the author's estimate.

process_map.name: Communicate outages to customers
process_map.description: Outage information from the OMS feeds the outage map, IVR messages and social media, and during large outages communications advisors post regular updates with estimated restoration times and safety warnings. Accurate estimates depend on crews reporting damage assessments promptly. During the 2022 storm the utility issued several updates a day for more than a week.

evidence.note: Storm update releases (src6, src7); ordinary volume is the author's estimate.

surge.cause: major storm (wind, ice storm, tornado or derecho)

evidence.note: The May 2022 derecho caused more than 1,000 outages, five times the 2018 tornadoes, with restoration over about ten days (src6, src7); 2021 had one major event (src1). Frequency and multiplier ranges are the author's estimate.

process_map.name: Handle claims and damage recovery
process_map.description: Legal staff handle claims against the utility for damage from outages, voltage events, vehicle accidents and construction, working with the insurer, and recover repair costs from drivers and excavators who damage poles and cable. Recovery needs complete crew cost records and police or locate evidence.

evidence.note: Typical; volume is the author's estimate.

process_map.name: Set strategy and govern through the board
process_map.description: The executive team prepares the strategic direction, business plan and budget for the board of directors, which answers to the municipal shareholder; the board approves the capital plan, rate applications, financing and dividends. Board cycles run quarterly with committee meetings in between. Shareholder expectations on dividends and rates frame every plan; the City received a $23.7M dividend in 2021.

evidence.note: Strategic direction (src3) and dividend (src11).

process_map.name: Manage enterprise risk
process_map.description: The risk advisor maintains the enterprise risk register with named owners: severe weather, cyber attack, workforce retirements, aging assets, regulatory decisions and the pandemic, and reports ratings and mitigations to executives and the audit committee. Major incidents and audit findings update the register between reviews.

evidence.note: Risks named in src3.

process_map.name: Run internal audits
process_map.description: Internal auditors run a risk-based audit plan covering billing, procurement, payroll, capital project controls and IT access, test controls and report findings and agreed actions to the audit committee. Follow-up of overdue actions is a standing agenda item.

evidence.note: Typical for a municipal utility; volume is the author's estimate.

sources.supports: Hydro Ottawa has nearly 5,000 km of underground cable, more than 90% XLPE, much installed from the mid-1970s to 1990 and at or past its 30-year expected life; replacing on faults is a lagging approach; injection versus replacement depends on splice count and feasibility.

sources.title: How we fix underground cable faults
sources.supports: Cable faults mostly from age and dig-ins, more frequent in spring and summer; fuse operates, crew uses a thumper to find the fault, customers switched to an alternate feed where possible, return visit a day or two later, other utilities located before digging, excavation with high-pressure water, cut out and splice, backfill; full repair takes several days depending on locates and excavation.

sources.title: Rules for electricity utilities

sources.supports: Planned Hydro One loss of supply to three stations plus a defective-equipment outage; 9,186 customers; 90% restored in 6.8 h; customers notified four days before; dedicated switching crew; weekly preparation meeting for on-call managers; daily SAIDI 12.1 against a threshold of 5.14.

assumptions: The organisation is a composite modelled mainly on Hydro Ottawa Limited in 2019-2022. Customer, asset, financial, service quality and reliability figures are that company's published numbers; the organisation chart, role split, headcounts, wages and most process volumes are the author's estimates.

Corporate functions (HR, IT, finance, legal, communications, fleet and facilities) are shown inside the distribution company. Hydro Ottawa reported 581 FTE for 2020 (668 in the holding company). Role headcounts were about 570 until 2026-11-24, when roles were raised to the work the workflows record, giving 658 employees, about 13% above the reported FTE. Either some workflow volumes and step times are high, or more work is contracted out than the file shows; locates are already shown as contracted.

Loaded cost per hour = 2019-2022 hourly wage x 1.40 for benefits, OMERS pension, payroll taxes and overhead. Lineworker rates start from the Job Bank 2024-2025 Ontario median (src9) scaled back about 8% to the reference period; other wages are estimates for Ottawa-area utilities.

Volumes with no published figure (outage events, trouble calls, locates, move-ins, billing exceptions, arrears accounts, inspections) are tier C estimates and should be replaced with company data where available.

Distribution System Code inspection cycles, the Ontario One Call five-business-day locate deadline, OESP and LEAP rules and Measurement Canada sampling rules are described from general knowledge; their source pages were not opened.
The model uses monthly billing of all customers, consistent with more than 4.2 million bills for about 350,000 customers in 2021 (src1).

Storm surges use the May 2022 derecho (180,000 customers affected, more than 1,000 outages, about 400 poles, ten days) as the large ordinary case and assume one to four declared major events a year; 2021 had one (src1).

Pandemic effects in 2020-2022 (remote office work, hiring freeze, suspended non-critical projects, disconnection pauses and relief credits) are mentioned where they changed a process but are not modelled as a separate state.
